reviews.text: That opening sequence is fantastic. The whole one-shot concept grabbed me immediately, and the cinematography is incredible. But who really wants to sit through almost two hours of World War I? After the initial wow factor wore off, this became a bit of a snooze fest for me. Beautifully made, technically impressive, great performances—but watching two guys slog through trenches, mud, explosions and misery for two hours just wasn’t doing it for me. Maybe if I’d grown up hearing World War I stories from my grandparents or great-grandparents, or if there were a couple of major stars carrying me through it, I’d feel differently. But it’s a bunch of characters I have no connection to, fighting a war that feels increasingly distant. At this point, historical war dramas like this feel less like entertainment and more like an Ambien.

The "one take" gimmick makes it look and feel like a third-person-video game. The story and characters are one cliché after another. And, of course, it's pro-war propaganda.

It's pretty awesome that the entire movie is one take, but because of that, they weren't able to take as many risks, and that hurts the film. It's incredibly slow, and even the final payoff isn't nearly good enough to make up for that. The cinematography is obviously impressive, but the technical achievement becomes more interesting than the actual story. The characters aren't particularly compelling, and the dialogue does little to make the long stretches of the movie engaging.

Deux soldats britanniques, Schofield et Blake, envoyés livrer un simple message pour annuler une attaque programmée à l'aube, la mission de coursier la plus stressante jamais confiée à deux mecs qui pensaient s'engager pour de la vraie guerre avec de vrais combats, et qui se retrouvent plutôt embarqués dans un marathon chronométré à travers un no man's land rempli de pièges, de rats géants et de cadavres, sans même une pause hydratation ni un GPS pour les guider, l'armée britannique version course d'orientation extrême, sponsorisée par l'angoisse permanente. Mendes mise tout sur son plan-séquence continu, prouesse technique folle sur le papier, mais qui finit par montrer deux silhouettes courir sans jamais laisser le temps de s'attacher à elles. La traversée de la rivière reste le seul vrai moment d'immersion réussi. La scène nocturne dans la ville en flammes, censée être le climax, sent trop le décor de studio pour convaincre. Bref, une prouesse technique qui privilégie la mise en scène à l'attachement humain, et qui rate son morceau de bravoure le plus important, 1 étoile.

I loved the one continues shot this movie had no cuts or anything. However, the movie has one of the worse plots I have seen in a war movie. The emotional scenes feel dry and the action seems boring. War epic that spans the entire brutal reality of trench warfare through one continuous, unbroken feeling journey across enemy lines, honestly the technical achievement never overshadows genuine human stakes underneath the spectacle throughout. Nothing about the mission stays clean or heroic. Sound design does enormous immersive work throughout every chaotic confrontation depicted here. The scale of the technical achievement never overshadows genuine human stakes underneath the spectacle throughout. This remains genuinely harrowing, technically remarkable filmmaking, confident enough to let confusion and terror carry weight. I finished mostly out of stubbornness rather than any real investment by the last stretch. Solid watch overall, worth the time.

Whatever. I’m so tired of post 2000s American/Western war films. They offer nothing new, nothing that hasn’t been said before. War is now used to give an actor/director an Oscar. To let them try out a new piece of equipment. Though I guess it’s always been like that. Aside from the no cut close third person view, though there are many cuts, that feels like a video game, this is more focused on experience and being described as “if you were at war” trying to get a mental or physical reaction out of people watching this in the theaters. It wants to be called immersive so bad. It offers  nothing new on WW1 or wars at all. The talk about how they go home in a casket but have a medal to show for it, the fighting over acres of land. Everything i’ve already seen, heard, and read. Gets tired after a while, our two main guys are fine. Conversations are nothing. There’s praise for its friendship and camaraderie but that’s always in war films, and this one’s also surface level. It looks good I guess but if I wanted to see pretty scenes about war there’s plenty of paintings about that. I should’ve watched the Fifth Seal instead.

Not a fan. It felt like a theme park ride. Specifically one of those dark rides at an amusement park. You're just moved from one set piece to another with a thin objective as to why you're being moved around. The whole movie felt like it was on a rail. I couldn't get past that, and given how predictable the events of the movie are, it wasn't an exciting ride. I felt it mostly had to do with the continuous take mechanism. Its the dominating trait of the movie, and much like Rope, its an impressive process and the cuts are cleverly hidden. I can't imagine how many things had to go right for the end product to look this seamless. And to see the camera somehow keep up no matter what scene its in was cool. It's great cinematography, it shined the most in the burning village halfway into the movie. And the technical work behind the movie is still impressive: the expansive & detailed sets, as well as the huge number of extras (epic in scale, but for a simple 1hr50 movie!). But beyond that, I couldn't find anything noteworthy about the movie. Once you see what the movie is trying to do with the continuous take, it quickly wears off and becomes a gimmick, and then starts actively drawing attention to itself, almost like it's to distract from how thin the story actually is and how lacking it is in substance. I cannot name one notable thing that happened in the first hour - actually, in the entire movie - anything that makes me want to rewatch it. Put aside the continuous shot gimmick and there's just not much left to the movie itself. Even the climatic run during the attack, and the ending itself were both really underwhelming. The dialogue was dull, the emotional moments were predictable and manipulative, the bad guys were just cartoonishly evil obstacles, the sound design was drowned out by the score, I eventually couldn't wait for the whole thing to end. It felt like the movie has no substance beyond its continuous shot style. Overall, it was really underwhelming.

The set design and visuals were impressive, however everything else was a bit lacklustre. The main runners came across as super soft and needed to say everything they were thinking - leaving nothing for the viewer to infer (boring). Although the filming technique was creative, it felt gimicky when the other elements of a captivating film were missing.

É um filme que impressiona muito pelo visual. A fotografia é incrível, os cenários são muito bem feitos e o plano-sequência dá a sensação de que tudo está acontecendo em tempo real. Tecnicamente, é um filme muito bonito e dá para entender por que recebeu tantos elogios. Mesmo assim, a história não me conquistou. Em vários momentos tive a sensação de que o filme se resumia ao protagonista andando de um lugar para outro, e isso acabou deixando o ritmo repetitivo para mim. Eu esperava mais acontecimentos e um desenvolvimento que me envolvesse mais com a missão. No fim não foi suficiente para tornar a experiência realmente interessante. É um filme bonito de assistir, porém achei a narrativa fraca e pouco envolvente.

I saw this film on its first release in 2020 and I see from my history gave it 2.5 stars (indifferent/ mediocre). It’s one of the films where I find myself quite a bit out of step with the Letterboxd consensus, so I eventually got round to a re-watch to find out what I was missing. I have decided to revisit my mark - by knocking 1/2 mark off (2 stars = bad but not awful, so it has a redeeming feature). Given that there are many others who love this movie (and I appreciate that some of those have actually war experience and so cannot be dismissed), let me try to explain. Technically, this film is outstanding. The cinematography by the great Roger Deakins, the editing by Lee Smith, the lighting and the sound design - all beyond reproach. They all contribute to the apparent single shot presentation which is, at least as a technical achievement, rightly much lauded. At least in the first act and toward the end of the third this presentation drew me in and made the film seem immersive. But for me that is where it ends. This is a film that almost screams “Look how brilliant the director/ cinematographer/ sound is” in every moment at the cost of everything else. The plot is thin, contains far too many unlikely coincidences and events requiring a total suspension of belief. In particular there is a scene with a French woman and child that is tacky and adds nothing to the plot or action. The plot also drags a bit in places and it really needed to be faster paced. There are some fine cameos, particularly by Andrew Scott, Mark Strong and Benedict Cumberbatch, but the leads are ill-served by the script. This is a world populated by stereotypes - the Germans are all (very) bad,  the serving man the suffering salt of the earth. Beyond that there is no characterisation to speak of, and the lead character(s) are uncharismatic and totally emotionless. By the end of the film, I didn’t care what happened to anyone. There are of course other one shot presentation films - Birdman and Rope spring to mind - but none on the scale of this. For that reason, I suspect that 1917 might be on the syllabus of film courses for years to come. If I had been marking this film solely on technical achievement, certainly a 4.5, possibly a 5. But for the casual viewer, this is basically a gimmick film that is all about spectacle and special effects - more of an experience than a narrative film and you may find your attention wandering long before the end. While I admire the craft, I cannot recommend it to other than film students.

I think this is so trite and overdrawn that it took me three attempts to finish through. Beyond the technical achievements of the film, much of the experience is bogged down by pacing issues and shallow dramaturgy, thoroughly reliant on a flimsy emotional stake that simply never stuck deep enough to elevate the otherwise amazing set pieces. Formally, too, there's almost no reason to invest any interest, as it never really moves past the gimmick of a oner, nor does it have the balls to fully commit to the bit. The camera wanders around and swings past our characters, but it feels more like a cam op hitting their marks rather than a fleshed out visual direction; it simply stages the next set-piece for us to see. The only time that the camera does feel like an actual cinematic instrument was in the trenches, where the claustrophobic corridors and shifting uniformed bodies serve to juxtapose the movements our characters are making; opposite against the huddled safety of the masses, away from the high walls of the trenches, into the open air of death. I should watch Dunkirk again.

1917, c'est un plan séquence de deux heures. On est toujours dans le feu de l'action, spectateur en première loge. Comme pour un DJ set sur vinyles, j'ai de l'admiration pour la technique et la passion que ça demande. Évidemment, la photographie de Roger Dickens est magnifique. Avec lui, le film ne pouvait pas vraiment se tromper. Ce que Sam Mendes réussit brillamment, c'est de rendre quelque chose d'aussi ennuyeux et pathétique que le vrai quotidien de la guerre en quelque chose de grandiose et épique, sans dénaturer son réalisme. Quatre-vingt-quinze pour cent de la merde vient de tout sauf de la guerre en elle-même. Et surtout : la guerre, ce n'est pas des mouvements de foule et de la stratégie militaire comme dans un jeu vidéo. C'est un bordel sans nom où tout peut dépendre du sprint d'une seule personne et du courant de la rivière. Le seul bémol, c'est les personnages principaux. Je ne me suis pas vraiment attaché à eux. À partir de ce là, c'est très très dur de ressentir des émotions humaines. On se limite aux émotions cinématographiques : la tension, l'inspiration, l'admiration... Des émotions qu'on ne vit qu'au cinéma.
